segments.translit: /chos thams cad khong du chud pa'i don de nyid sems can rnams kyi phyir grub pa'i slob dpon tha ga pa'i zhabs kyis gsungs te/
segments.translation: That very meaning, the understanding of all [dharmas]{dharma}, the [siddha]{siddha} master [Tantrīpāda]{p-tantri} spoke for the sake of beings:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song as spoken for the sake of beings by the [siddha]{siddha} master [Tantrīpāda]{p-tantri}, whom the Tibetan here calls tha ga pa'i zhabs, 'the venerable weaver'. Its meaning, he says, is the understanding of all [dharmas]{dharma} (cp.25.m1). His comment on this song survives only in the Tibetan translation.

flags.note: This comment survives only in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293); what is given is a translation of the Tibetan, and there is no Sanskrit to compare. The Sanskrit can be inferred only through the Tibetan: grub pa'i slob dpon presumably renders siddhācārya, khong du chud pa perhaps adhigama or avabodha, and don de nyid perhaps Munidatta's usual tam evārtham (cp.25.m1).

don de nyid is 'that very meaning' or 'that same meaning'. If it renders tam evārtham, as in Munidatta's openings to other songs, it means 'the same meaning' as before, and chos thams cad khong du chud pa'i may describe the poet ('who has understood all dharmas') rather than the meaning. I followed the plainer reading of the Tibetan genitive: the meaning that is the understanding of all dharmas (cp.25.m1).

Munidatta's comment names the poet tha ga pa'i zhabs, 'the venerable weaver' (cp.25.m1), while the song's heading has thag pa'i zhabs (thag pa, 'rope, cord'). Both are rendered by the glossary's Tantrīpāda. The Sanskrit name (tantrī, 'string, cord') does not occur in this text; it is inferred through the Tibetan and tradition. The English loses the echo of the refrain's 'weaver' (tha ga).

segments.translit: chos zhes bya ba la sogs pa ni chos 'byung dgongs pa'i skad kyis shes rab kyi chos 'byung du rtogs par bya'o/ /rkang rten zhes pa ni rkang pa bzhi dga' ba bzhi'i rten du gyur pa'o/ /de bzhin du brtag pa gnyis pa las kyang / i yig gang byed lha mo yi/ /zhes bya ba la sogs pa gsungs so/ /yang na don dam rig pas yang dag pa ji lta ba bzhin du gyur pa'i chos kyi 'byung gnas gang yin pa de ni chos 'byung ngo / /rdo rje zhes pa ni rnal 'byor gyi dbang phyug gi bya ba dang byed pa'i dngos po las de'i gnas kyi skad de ni rnal 'byor ro/ /de bzhin du sa ra ha'i zhabs kyis kyang / rdo rje 'bebs pas g.yo ba nyid/ /pad+ma yod pas rdo rje'o/ /bya ba byed pas rgyas 'debs pa/ /'di ni bde chen rgyal po'o/ /de la shes rab kyi chu skyes la me long lta bu la sogs pa'i ye shes lnga'i bdag nyid kun rdzob byang chub kyi sems ni stong pa nyid dang snying rje'i bdag nyid rdo rje bla ma'i drin las so/ /dri med gos zhes pa ni rang bzhin gyis 'od gsal gyis yongs su dag par byed do zhes so/ /de bzhin du brtag pa gnyis pa las kyang / kun rdzob kun+da dang mtshungs pa/ /don dam bde ba'i gzugs can no/ /zhes so/
segments.translation: “The [dharmodaya]{dharmodaya}…” and so on: in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}, the dharmodaya is to be understood as the dharmodaya of [wisdom]{prajna}. “[Footrest]{footrest}” means the four feet that have become the support of the four [joys]{ananda}. So too the [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra} says, “The [goddess]{devi}'s letter i, which makes…” and so on. Or else: whatever is the source of the [dharmas]{dharma} that, through awareness of the [ultimate]{paramartha}, have become just as they truly are, that is the dharmodaya. “[Vajra]{vajra}”: from the state of act and agent belonging to the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}, the voice of its place, that is yoga. So too [Saraha]{p-saraha} says: “By bringing down the vajra, there is movement; / because the [lotus]{lotus} is there, it is the vajra; / doing the act, it seals: / this is the king of [great bliss]{mahasukha}.” There, in the [lotus]{lotus} of [wisdom]{prajna}, [conventional]{samvrti} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, whose nature is the [five wisdoms]{pancajnana} beginning with [mirror-like wisdom]{adarsajnana}, has the nature of [emptiness]{sunyata} and [compassion]{karuna} through the [grace]{prasada} of the [vajra]{vajra} [guru]{guru}. “Stainless [cloth]{cloth}” means: it is made wholly pure by natural [clear light]{prabhasvara}. So too the [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra} says: “The [conventional]{samvrti} is like [jasmine]{kunda}; / the [ultimate]{paramartha} has the form of [bliss]{sukha}.”
segments.note: Munidatta reads the [dharmodaya]{dharmodaya}, in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}, as the dharmodaya of [wisdom]{prajna}, or as the source of dharmas become as they truly are; the [footrest]{footrest} as four feet supporting the four [joys]{ananda}; the voice of the vajra's place as yoga; and the stainless [cloth]{cloth} as what natural [clear light]{prabhasvara} makes wholly pure (cp.25.m2).

equations.en: in twilight language, the dharmodaya of wisdom (shes rab kyi chos 'byung)
or else, the source (chos kyi 'byung gnas) of the dharmas that, through awareness of the ultimate, have become just as they truly are
the four feet (rkang pa bzhi) that have become the support of the four joys

flags.note: This comment survives only in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293); what is given is a translation of the Tibetan, and there is no Sanskrit to compare. Sanskrit behind Munidatta's terms can be inferred only through the Tibetan (cp.25.m2): chos 'byung for dharmodaya, dgongs pa'i skad for sandhyābhāṣā, brtag pa gnyis pa for the Dvikalpa (Hevajra), kun rdzob byang chub kyi sems for saṃvṛtibodhicitta, rang bzhin gyis 'od gsal for prakṛtiprabhāsvara; the word behind rkang rten, 'footrest', cannot be recovered. Only kun+da (kunda) is transliterated. The jasmine line is the Hevajra's familiar comparison of the conventional to kunda; I have not been able to check its Sanskrit from the pack.

The Hevajra quotation (cp.25.m2) has i yig, 'the letter i' (ཨི). In the yoginī tantras it is the letter e (ཨེ), triangular, that stands for the dharmodaya, and the two vowel signs are easily confused, so e yig may be meant; I translate the text as it stands. The line is cut off by 'and so on', and its syntax is uncertain: 'the goddess's letter i, which makes…' or 'the letter i, which the goddess makes…'.

The sentence on 'vajra' (rdo rje zhes pa ni … rnal 'byor ro) is obscure (cp.25.m2). I take bya ba dang byed pa'i dngos po as 'the state (or relation) of act and agent', perhaps for a Sanskrit compound in -bhāva, and the final rnal 'byor as 'yoga' (union); it could also be 'the yogi'. What is equated seems to be 'the voice of its place', the vajra's place of 1a, with yoga. The Saraha verse that follows ('doing the act, it seals') suggests sexual union, but Munidatta does not say so.

The sentence on conventional bodhicitta (de la shes rab kyi chu skyes la … rdo rje bla ma'i drin las so) has no main verb (cp.25.m2). I read one statement: in the lotus of wisdom, conventional bodhicitta, of the nature of the five wisdoms, has the nature of emptiness and compassion through the vajra guru's grace. It may instead be two: bodhicitta has the nature of the five wisdoms; emptiness and compassion come from the guru's grace. dag par byed in the cloth gloss is active with no subject; I render it 'is made pure'.

Munidatta names the five wisdoms in his comment on couplet 1, whose second line has lan lnga, 'five times', but he does not cite lan lnga or 'thag cing 'thag pas, and he does not tie the five wisdoms to them (cp.25.m2). He cites 1a by its first syllable only (chos zhes bya ba la sogs pa), rendered here 'The dharmodaya…'. brtag pa gnyis pa, 'the Two Sections', is rendered by the glossary's Hevajra.

segments.translit: /dhrU'i rkang pas yang dag par rtogs pa brtan par byed do/ /bdag ni tha ga zhes bya ba la sogs pa ni ngo bo nyid kyi thabs kyi bdag ni tha ga pa'i zhabs so/ /rgyu dang spun dag gi gang gi phyir na kun rdzob dang don dam pa'i dbye ba dmigs pas mtshon pa dag gis mi shes so/ /de bzhin du yang / gzung 'dzin dngos po med pa'i phyir/ /sems ni gang du'ang skye ba med/ /gang la sems nyid skye med pa/ /de nyid mchog gi go 'phang ngo /
segments.translation: With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he makes right realization firm. “I am … a [weaver]{weaver}” and so on: the “I”, the self of [means]{upaya} by nature, is [Tantrīpāda]{p-tantri}. As for the [warp]{warp} and the [weft]{weft}: it is because those who mark by apprehending a distinction between the [conventional]{samvrti} and the [ultimate]{paramartha} do not know. So too: “Since [the grasped and the grasper]{grahya-grahaka} do not exist as things, / [mind]{citta} is not born anywhere at all; / where mind itself is unborn, / that is the supreme state.”
segments.note: Munidatta says the [refrain]{dhruvapada} makes right realization firm. Its 'I' is [Tantrīpāda]{p-tantri} himself, the self of [means]{upaya} by nature. On [warp]{warp} and [weft]{weft} he says that those who mark by apprehending a distinction of [conventional]{samvrti} and [ultimate]{paramartha} do not know, and adds a verse: where [mind]{citta} is unborn, that is the supreme state (cp.25.m3).

equations.src: bdag ni tha ga ('I … a weaver')
equations.en: the 'I' is Tantrīpāda himself (tha ga pa'i zhabs), the self of means by nature (ngo bo nyid kyi thabs kyi bdag)

citations.quoted: Since the grasped and the grasper do not exist as things, / mind is not born anywhere at all; / where mind itself is unborn, / that is the supreme state.
citations.work: not named (introduced only by 'so too'); not identified

flags.note: On 2b (spun dog): Munidatta cites the pair as rgyu dang spun dag (cp.25.m3). Dag is the plural particle, matching rgyu rnams, 'the warps', in 2a; this suggests the line's spun dog is a slip for spun dag, 'the wefts', with spun a noun. He does not gloss spun, so his wording does not confirm 'weft' against the ordinary sense 'siblings', though keeping rgyu and spun as a pair suits warp and weft. His clause ends mtshon pa dag gis mi shes so, 'those who mark do not know', with no bdag gir, 'as my own': a paraphrase, or a text in which the not-knowing belonged to those who mark dualistically rather than to the poet. It does not settle the subject of 2b.

rgyu dang spun dag gi gang gi phyir na … mi shes so is loose: a genitive pair followed by 'because' (cp.25.m3). I render 'As for warp and weft: it is because…'. Munidatta does not equate warp and weft with anything; the drift seems to be that the weaver does not take them as his own, since those who mark by apprehending a distinction of conventional and ultimate do not know.

This comment survives only in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293); what is given is a translation of the Tibetan, and there is no Sanskrit to compare. dhrU'i rkang pa transliterates dhruva(pada), so that term is secure; elsewhere the Sanskrit can be inferred only through the Tibetan (cp.25.m3): ngo bo nyid kyi thabs kyi bdag perhaps for a compound of svabhāva, upāya and ātman, gzung 'dzin for grāhyagrāhaka; nothing can be inferred for rgyu and spun. brtan par byed, 'makes firm', right after dhrU, may echo dhruva, 'fixed, firm'.

The comment's tha ga pa'i zhabs, 'the venerable weaver', is rendered by the glossary's Tantrīpāda (cp.25.m3); the point of the gloss, that the refrain's weaver is the poet, is clearer in the Tibetan than in the English.

segments.translit: /rkang pa gnyis pas rten dang brtan pa gsungs te/ phyed bcas khru gsum zhes bya ba la sogs pa ni rang gi lus la bsam gtan gyi khang par grol ba ste/ de la dga' ba gsum pa bskyed pa'o/ /nam mkha' khengs gyur zhes pa ni yongs su dag pa'i 'od gsal gyis yongs su sbyar bar byas pas so sor lta ba dang ldan pas bdag gnas pa'o/ /de bzhin du brtag pa gnyis pa las kyang / lus dang bral ba'i sems nyid ni/ /gzhan du spang bar bya ba med/ /ces so/
segments.translation: With the second [verse]{pada} he speaks of the support and of steadiness. “[Three and a half cubits]{three-and-a-half-cubits}…” and so on: in one's own [body]{body}, being released into the [house]{house} of meditation; there the third [joy]{ananda} is produced. “The [sky]{gagana} is filled” means: having been wholly joined with wholly purified [clear light]{prabhasvara}, I abide, endowed with discerning vision. So too the [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra} says: “[Mind]{citta} itself, apart from the [body]{body}, / is not to be given up elsewhere.”
segments.note: Munidatta takes the second verse as speaking of support and steadiness: the [three and a half cubits]{three-and-a-half-cubits} are one's own [body]{body}, where one is released into the house of meditation and the third [joy]{ananda} arises; the [sky]{gagana} is filled when one, wholly joined with purified [clear light]{prabhasvara}, abides with discerning vision (cp.25.m4).

equations.src: phyed bcas khru gsum (three and a half cubits)
equations.en: one's own body (rang gi lus), in which one is released into the house of meditation and the third joy is produced

equations.src: nam mkha' khengs gyur (the sky is filled)
equations.en: having been wholly joined with wholly purified clear light, abiding endowed with discerning vision

citations.quoted: Mind itself, apart from the body, / is not to be given up elsewhere.
citations.work: Hevajra Tantra, cited as brtag pa gnyis pa (the Dvikalpa); the verse is not located

flags.note: On 3a (sun sgron gsum): Munidatta cites 3a only as phyed bcas khru gsum 'and so on' and neither quotes nor glosses sun sgron gsum (cp.25.m4). His paraphrase runs: one's own body, the house of meditation (bsam gtan gyi khang pa, perhaps answering the line's khyim, 'house'), being released (grol ba), the third joy (dga' ba gsum pa). Nothing in it speaks of lamps, so it gives no support to 'three lamps'. If 'the third joy' answers the line's final gsum, he took the number as an ordinal tied to the joys; whether grol ba answers sgron cannot be told. His citation confirms 3b's nam mkha' khengs gyur as transmitted.

Several phrases are uncertain (cp.25.m4). rten dang brtan pa, 'support and steadiness', may mean the body as support and the steadiness reached in it. bdag gnas pa'o may be 'I abide' (the poet speaking, as in cp.25.m5 and cp.25.m6) or 'abides as oneself'. so sor lta ba, 'discerning vision', may render pratyavekṣaṇā. grol ba, 'released', sits oddly with 'into the house of meditation'; a scribal slip cannot be excluded.

The Hevajra verse Munidatta quotes (lus dang bral ba'i sems nyid ni / gzhan du spang bar bya ba med, cp.25.m4) is ambiguous: 'mind itself, apart from the body, is not to be given up elsewhere', or 'there is nothing elsewhere to give up: mind itself, free of the body'. In context it seems to support placing the practice in one's own body. I have not located the verse.

This comment survives only in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293); what is given is a translation of the Tibetan, and there is no Sanskrit to compare. The Sanskrit can be inferred only through the Tibetan (cp.25.m4): rkang pa gnyis pa for dvitīyapada, his 'second verse' (couplet 3); phyed bcas khru gsum for some 'three and a half hastas'; bsam gtan gyi khang pa for a dhyāna 'house' or hall (a guess); dga' ba gsum pa for the third of the four joys, which joy depending on the system's order; 'od gsal for prabhāsvara.

segments.translit: /rkang pa gsum pas yid ches pa'i tshogs pa gsungs te/ gzhom du med pa zhes bya ba la sogs pa'i thags bzangs ni dgongs pa'i skad kyis srog dang rtsol ba thabs dang shes rab kyi bdag nyid kyis rlung gnyis la gzhom du med pa'i sgra dang gzugs brnyan yongs su rtog pa zhes so/ /lhan cig skyes pa'i sgra brnyan dang / /de nyid kun rdzob byang chub kyi sems bla ma dam pa'i gsung gis bsgrub par bya'o/ /gnas gnyis chad gyur zhes pa ni dngos po dngos po med par 'dzin pa dag bcad nas rdo rje dang chu skyes yang dag par sbyor ba bstan pas mi phyed par bdag gis bya'o zhes so/
segments.translation: With the third [verse]{pada} he speaks of the gathering of conviction. The [fine weave]{fine-weave} of “[Unstruck]{anahata}…” and so on means, in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}: through [prāṇa and āyāma]{pranayama}, whose nature is [means]{upaya} and [wisdom]{prajna}, fully imagining in the two [winds]{vayu} the unstruck sound and the image. The [innate]{sahaja} echo, and that very [conventional]{samvrti} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, are to be accomplished through the word of the true [guru]{guru}. “The [two places]{two-places} cut” means: having cut off the graspings at [being and nonbeing]{bhava-abhava}, through the teaching of the right union of [vajra]{vajra} and [lotus]{lotus}, I am to make it inseparable.
segments.note: Munidatta calls the [unstruck]{anahata} [fine weave]{fine-weave} [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}: through [prāṇa and āyāma]{pranayama}, which are means and wisdom, one imagines unstruck sound and image in the two [winds]{vayu}; the true [guru]{guru}'s word accomplishes the innate echo and conventional bodhicitta. Cutting the [two places]{two-places} is cutting off grasping at being and nonbeing, then making the union of vajra and lotus inseparable (cp.25.m5).

equations.src: thags bzangs (fine weave), cited with gzhom du med pa (unstruck)
equations.en: in twilight language: through prāṇa and āyāma, of the nature of means and wisdom, fully imagining the unstruck sound and the image in the two winds

equations.src: srog dang rtsol ba (prāṇa and āyāma)
equations.en: means and wisdom (thabs dang shes rab), in that order

equations.src: gnas gnyis chad gyur (the two places cut)
equations.en: the graspings at being and nonbeing (dngos po dngos po med par 'dzin pa), which are cut off

flags.note: On 4a (sbra): Munidatta cites the phrase as gzhom du med pa … thags bzangs, spelling thags, 'woven cloth', which supports 'fine weave' against the line's thag (cp.25.m5). He then speaks of gzhom du med pa'i sgra, 'the unstruck sound', of sgra dang gzugs brnyan, 'sound and image', and of sgra brnyan, 'echo', and never of a tent. This supports the conjecture sgra, 'sound', for the line's sbra, though 'unstruck sound' is a stock phrase and he may only be expanding gzhom med. His 'to be accomplished through the true guru's word' (bla ma dam pa'i gsung gis bsgrub par bya) answers the line's 'not apart from the guru's word' (bla ma'i gsung bral min).

On 4b: Munidatta cites the line as gnas gnyis chad gyur, 'the two places severed', where it reads gnas gnyis bcad nas, 'having cut the two places' (cp.25.m5); his text had another verb form, though the sense is close. He does not cite rgyun, bsgrims or sgyongs. In their place his gloss has the right union of vajra and lotus and 'I am to make it inseparable' (mi phyed par bdag gis bya'o), an act the speaker performs. That would suit an imperative such as skyongs, 'keep, maintain', for sgyongs, but it is only compatible with it, not evidence for it. Nothing in it bears on rgyun.

yid ches pa'i tshogs pa, literally 'the gathering of conviction', is odd as Munidatta's heading for the third verse (cp.25.m5). If the Sanskrit had pratyaya, 'conviction' but also 'condition', with sāmagrī, 'assemblage', it may have meant 'the assemblage of conditions'. This is a guess made through the Tibetan only. I translate the Tibetan.

yongs su rtog pa, 'fully imagining' (parikalpanā?), might be a slip for yongs su rtogs pa, 'fully realizing'; I follow the text (cp.25.m5). lhan cig skyes pa'i sgra brnyan dang / / is punctuated like a verse line and may be a quoted fragment; I read it as prose. mi phyed par bdag gis bya'o has no object: 'I am to make it (the union) inseparable' or 'I am to act without division'.

This comment survives only in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293); what is given is a translation of the Tibetan, and there is no Sanskrit to compare. The Sanskrit can be inferred only through the Tibetan (cp.25.m5): gzhom du med pa for anāhata; srog dang rtsol ba for prāṇāyāma, divided into srog, 'life', and rtsol ba, 'exertion', which suggests Munidatta treated prāṇa and āyāma as a pair; thabs dang shes rab for upāya and prajñā; sgra brnyan, 'echo', and gzugs brnyan, 'image', perhaps for pratiśrutkā and pratibimba; lhan cig skyes pa for sahaja; dngos po dngos po med pa for bhāva and abhāva.

segments.translit: /rkang pa bzhi pas rnal 'byor pa'i rjes su bsngags pa gsungs te/ nor bus son pa zhes bya ba la sogs pa ni chos thams cad rang bzhin gyis 'od gsal ba'i khong du chud pa las dar ma'i skye bo dang 'khyud pas de nyid rang bzhin gyis yongs su gyur pa a wa dhU tI rnal 'byor ma bdag med ma'o/ /nor bur gnas zhes pa ni 'thag pa'i tshul tha ga'i zhabs bdag gis thob pa'o/ /de'i phyir de'i drin las gti mug gis mngon par 'khyud pa'i srad bus bcings pa rnam par dral bar gyur pa'o/ /thag ces pa ni skyes pa'i chos dang rnam par bral nas rdo rje 'dzin par gyur to zhes pa'o/ /de bzhin du sa ra ha'i zhabs kyis kyang / de ni dpal ldan zhes bya ba la sogs pa gsungs so/
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada} he speaks the [praise]{anusamsa} of the [yogi]{yogi}. “Sown with the [jewel]{mani}…” and so on: from understanding all [dharmas]{dharma} as naturally [clear light]{prabhasvara}, through embracing the youthful one, that very one, wholly transformed by nature, is the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}, the [yoginī]{yogini} [Nairātmā]{nairatma}. “Abiding in the [jewel]{mani}” means: I, [Tantrīpāda]{p-tantri}, have obtained the way of [weaving]{weaving}. Therefore, by that one's [grace]{prasada}, the binding by the [thread]{thread} of [delusion]{moha}'s clinging embrace has been torn apart. “[Weaving]{weaving}” means: having parted from [dharmas]{dharma} that are born, he became [Vajradhara]{p-vajradhara}. So too [Saraha]{p-saraha} says, “That is glorious…” and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta calls the last verse praise of the [yogi]{yogi}: understanding all dharmas as naturally [clear light]{prabhasvara} and embracing a youthful one, that one becomes the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}, the yoginī [Nairātmā]{nairatma}. 'Abiding in the jewel' is the poet's gaining the way of [weaving]{weaving}; by that grace the binding [thread]{thread} of delusion is torn, and he becomes [Vajradhara]{p-vajradhara} (cp.25.m6).

flags.note: On 5a (nor bus son pa): Munidatta cites 5a as nor bus son pa, as the line has it, so the commentary's Tibetan already read these words (cp.25.m6). He does not gloss son pa, and nothing in his gloss concerns sowing: he speaks of embracing a youthful one, who becomes the avadhūtī, Nairātmā. He also cites nor bur gnas, 'abiding in the jewel', which the transmitted couplet lacks, so the verse he commented on differed from the one quoted; nor bur gnas may once have stood in 5a, perhaps where stong nyid kyis mtshon or stong nyid snying now stand. The draft's 'sown' remains unsupported.

de'i drin las, 'by that one's grace': the grace may be Nairātmā's, just named, or the guru's; the Tibetan does not say (cp.25.m6). dar ma'i skye bo, 'the youthful one', is unclear; it may be a young woman, the consort, and the Sanskrit (perhaps taruṇī or a word for youth) is a guess through the Tibetan.

rdo rje 'dzin par gyur (cp.25.m6): 'became Vajradhara', the buddha, or 'became a vajra-holder'; I link Vajradhara. The subject is unstated; 'he' might be 'I', continuing 'I, Tantrīpāda'. The cited word thag may be thag, 'weave', of 5b (thag gi ro rnyed), or a short form of tha ga, 'weaver'.

Where 5b has the weaver freed (grol) from the net (dra ba) of delusion, Munidatta speaks of the binding by the thread (srad bu) of delusion's clinging embrace, torn apart (rnam par dral) (cp.25.m6). Image and verb differ: dral may echo dra ba or grol, or reflect a different reading of the line.

This comment survives only in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293); what is given is a translation of the Tibetan, and there is no Sanskrit to compare. The Sanskrit can be inferred only through the Tibetan (cp.25.m6): rjes su bsngags pa for anuśaṃsā; a wa dhU tI transliterates avadhūtī, so that word is secure; rnal 'byor ma bdag med ma for Nairātmā yoginī; nor bu for maṇi; srad bu for sūtra; mngon par 'khyud pa perhaps for abhiṣvaṅga; rdo rje 'dzin pa for vajradhara.

questions: 2b (cp.25.m3): Munidatta's citation reads rgyu dang spun dag, with the plural dag matching rgyu rnams in 2a. Should the song draft read spun dag, 'the wefts', and note dog as a probable slip? His clause also lacks bdag gir ('as my own'); does the reviewer want the song's 'I do not know how to mark as my own' kept as is?

4a (cp.25.m5): his comment speaks only of the unstruck sound (sgra), sound and image, and echo, never of a tent, and spells thags bzangs. Is that enough to adopt sgra for sbra in the song draft (e.g. 'the sound of the unstruck fine weave is not apart from the guru's word'), or should 'tent' stand with a stronger flag?

4b: my own conjecture, not Munidatta's: rgyun rnams may be rgyu rnams, 'the warp threads', as in 2a, and sgyongs may be skyongs, 'keep, maintain'. His 'I am to make it inseparable' (cp.25.m5) fits an imperative but proves nothing. Can another Tengyur edition (Peking, Narthang, Golden) be checked for 3a, 4a, 4b and 5a?
5a (cp.25.m6): he cites nor bur gnas, 'abiding in the jewel', which the transmitted couplet lacks. Should the song draft carry a witness note that the commentary's verse text differed here?

Name (cp.25.m1, cp.25.m3, cp.25.m6): the comment calls the poet tha ga pa'i zhabs, 'the venerable weaver', so its gloss of the refrain ('the I is tha ga pa'i zhabs') is a pun on tha ga, 'weaver'. I used the glossary's Tantrīpāda throughout. Would the reviewer prefer 'the venerable Weaver' in the commentary, with Tantrīpāda in the note?
The Hevajra quotation in cp.25.m2 reads i yig, 'the letter i'; e yig, 'the letter e' (the triangular dharmodaya letter), seems likelier. I translated 'i' and flagged it. Emend?

Keep-source-first-gloss terms that first occur in this unit's commentary (siddha, bodhicitta, avadhūtī, prāṇa and āyāma; Nairātmā) have no first-occurrence gloss, since the weave schema has no notes array. Should the woven notes carry those glosses?

dngos po dngos po med pa in cp.25.m5: I linked the glossary's 'being and nonbeing' (bhava-abhava); the two-places entry's reading says 'things and non-things'. Which wording should the commentary use?
brtag pa gnyis pa (cp.25.m2, cp.25.m4) is rendered by the glossary's 'Hevajra'. Should the commentary keep the title Munidatta's Tibetan uses, 'the Dvikalpa', as a variant of tx-hevajra?
